questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a web crawler in a search engine?
options: To rank web pages by relevance
To discover and download web pages by following links across the internet
To serve search results to users
To compress web pages for faster loading
questions.explanation: A web crawler (spider) starts from seed URLs, downloads pages, extracts links from them, and follows those links to discover new pages. This process builds the corpus of web pages that the search engine can index and search.

questions.question: What is an inverted index?
options: A database that stores web pages in reverse chronological order
A data structure mapping each word to the list of documents containing it
An index that sorts documents by page size from largest to smallest
A backup copy of the search index stored in reverse order
questions.explanation: An inverted index maps every unique word to a posting list — the list of documents containing that word, often with positions and frequencies. Searching for a query means looking up each query term and intersecting their posting lists.

questions.question: What does TF-IDF measure?
options: The total number of pages on the internet
How relevant a term is to a document, balancing frequency in the document against commonness across all documents
The loading speed of a web page
The number of backlinks pointing to a page
questions.explanation: TF (Term Frequency) measures how often a term appears in a document. IDF (Inverse Document Frequency) penalizes terms that appear in many documents (like 'the'). Their product highlights terms that are frequent in a specific document but rare overall.

questions.question: How does PageRank determine the authority of a web page?
options: By counting the number of words on the page
By counting and weighting the incoming links from other pages, especially authoritative ones
By measuring how fast the page loads
By checking how recently the page was updated
questions.explanation: PageRank models the web as a graph. A page's rank is determined by the number and quality of pages linking to it. A link from an authoritative page (high PageRank) contributes more than a link from an obscure page. It's computed iteratively until convergence.

questions.question: Why do web crawlers use a politeness policy?
options: To ensure crawled content is family-friendly
To limit request rate per domain so crawling doesn't overwhelm web servers
To prioritize crawling government websites first
To only crawl pages written in English
questions.explanation: Politeness policies (often guided by robots.txt) limit how frequently a crawler hits a single domain. Without rate limiting, a crawler fetching thousands of pages per second could effectively DDoS a website. Crawlers introduce delays between requests to the same host.

questions.question: How is the search index distributed across thousands of servers?
options: Every server holds a complete copy of the entire index
The index is sharded so each server holds a portion; queries are broadcast to all shards in parallel
Servers are assigned to different geographic regions and only index local content
Only one server holds the index; others are backup replicas
questions.explanation: The index is far too large for one machine. It's sharded across thousands of servers, each holding a slice. A query is broadcast to all shards in parallel, each returns its top matches, and a coordinator merges and re-ranks the combined results.

questions.question: What data structure do crawlers commonly use to avoid re-visiting already-seen URLs?
options: A linked list of visited URLs
A bloom filter for fast probabilistic membership testing
A binary search tree sorted by URL length
A hash map with exact counts of visits per URL
questions.explanation: Bloom filters provide fast, space-efficient membership testing. They may produce false positives (claiming a URL was seen when it wasn't) but never false negatives. For billions of URLs, the space savings over a hash set are enormous.

questions.question: How does a search engine handle index freshness for breaking news?
options: It rebuilds the entire index every minute
It uses tiered indexing — a small real-time index for fresh content merged with a larger batch index at query time
It only indexes news sites and ignores the rest of the web
It relies on users to report stale results
questions.explanation: Tiered indexing maintains a small, frequently updated real-time index for fresh content (news, trending pages) alongside a larger batch index rebuilt periodically. Query results merge from both tiers, balancing freshness with comprehensive coverage.

questions.question: A search query is sent to 1000 index shards in parallel. Each shard has a p99 latency of 50ms. What is the expected tail latency for the complete query?
options: 50ms (same as each shard)
50,000ms (sum of all shards)
Significantly higher than 50ms due to tail-at-scale — the slowest of 1000 shards dominates
25ms (faster due to parallelism)
questions.explanation: With 1000 parallel shards, the query latency equals the slowest shard. The probability that at least one shard exceeds its p99 is extremely high (1 - 0.99^1000 is nearly 100%). This 'tail-at-scale' problem means the effective latency is far worse than any individual shard's p99.

questions.question: A search engine indexes 100 billion web pages. Each inverted index entry (word to document mapping) averages 100 bytes. The vocabulary contains 10 million unique words. Each word has an average posting list length of 1 million documents. Approximately how much storage does the index require?
options: 1 TB
10 TB
100 PB
questions.explanation: 10 million words x 1 million docs per word x 100 bytes per entry = 10^6 x 10^6 x 100 = 10^15 bytes = 1 PB. This is why the index must be sharded across thousands of machines, each holding a fraction of a petabyte.
